title: Application to Astrographer (graphical RAG engine + document store/wiki)
keyFindings: Astrographer's data model is already a knowledge graph: `fact`/`reference`/`content` nodes, `link`/`embed` edges, and node/edge properties (astrographer.md §4.2) — so Graph RAG is a retrieval behavior over the existing substrate, not a foreign addition.

The graph-enhanced vector search axis is already in the suite: Incanter's hybrid graph-tension + vector query (incanter.md §4.8) and Zodiac's graph/vector/hybrid modes (zodiac.md §4.3.2) are the vector+graph fusion seam.

The strongest Graph RAG fit is explainability/traceability: the consistency model already tracks every link/embed to its target (astrographer.md §4.2.3), so extending ragQuery results with a trace path directly answers the governance/sourcing point at low cost.

Relationship-aware, multi-hop retrieval over the reference→fact graph (topological resolution) is the core MUST-HAVE, consistent with the DAG-RAG research (dag-rag-research-notes.md §4) and D2 (runs locally over the Provident graph).

Expensive global techniques — community summaries (Microsoft GraphRAG global search) and dynamic graph query generation — are PARKED for D2 local-first cost/latency reasons and overlap with already-parked DAG-RAG items.

Secondary consumers inherit the graph layer indirectly: Familiar routes research through Astrographer's rag_query (familiar.md §4.3.3); Solomon and Mystery are PARKED until their search/crosslink semantics finalize.
summary: Graph RAG is not a foreign technique for the Auspicion Suite: Astrographer and Zodiac are already graphical RAG engines over knowledge-graph-shaped data (nodes/edges/properties). The concrete MUST/SHOULD work is graph-enhanced retrieval over Astrographer's reference graph (topological reference→fact resolution) plus an explainability/trace surface on RAG results, reusing the provenance the consistency model already tracks. Expensive global techniques (community summaries, dynamic graph query generation) stay PARKED for D2 local-first cost reasons.
